slides.tagline: Run a private AI chatbot entirely on your own PC
slides.lede: No cloud account, no subscription, no monthly bill. A beginner's walkthrough of Windows Subsystem for Linux, Ollama, and OpenWebUI — one command at a time.

slides.narration: Welcome. By the end of this deck you'll be running your own private AI chatbot, entirely on your own PC, with nothing sent to the cloud. We'll go through Windows Subsystem for Linux, Ollama, and OpenWebUI, one exact command at a time. No prior Linux experience needed.

slides.subtitle: Four stops, in order

items.label: Install WSL

items.label: Install Ollama

items.detail: Choose the right size AI model for your hardware

items.label: Install OpenWebUI

slides.narration: Here's the shape of the journey. First we install Windows Subsystem for Linux. Then we install Ollama inside it and learn its core commands. Next we pick an AI model sized right for your computer. And finally we install OpenWebUI, so you get a clean chat window in your browser instead of a bare terminal.

slides.heading: Before You Start
slides.subtitle: Windows 10 (build 19041+) or Windows 11, 64-bit, with virtualization enabled in BIOS/UEFI

stats.label: minimum — 16 GB+ recommended for bigger models
disk space for WSL plus your first model
any Intel or AMD chip from the last ~8 years

slides.narration: A quick reality check before we start. You'll need Windows 10 build 19041 or later, or Windows 11, both 64-bit, with virtualization turned on in your BIOS — it usually is by default. Plan on 8 gigabytes of RAM as a floor, 16 or more if you want to run bigger models comfortably, and about 20 gigabytes of free disk space to get through this whole walkthrough.

slides.heading: First, Some Vocabulary
slides.definition: Windows Subsystem for Linux — a real Linux environment that runs directly inside Windows. No virtual machine to set up, no dual-boot, no separate computer.
items: Files and networking are shared between Windows and Linux
This is where Ollama actually lives and runs
slides.narration: Let's define our first term. W-S-L stands for Windows Subsystem for Linux. It's a genuine Linux environment that runs directly inside Windows — no virtual machine to babysit, no dual-boot, no second computer. Files and networking are shared between the two sides, and this is where Ollama is actually going to live.

slides.heading: Install WSL
slides.subtitle: Five minutes, one restart

steps.title: Open PowerShell as Administrator
steps.detail: Right-click the Start button → Terminal (Admin), or search “PowerShell” and Run as administrator

steps.title: Run the install command
steps.detail: wsl --install

steps.title: Restart your computer
steps.detail: Windows will prompt you — save your work first

steps.title: Let Ubuntu finish setting up
steps.detail: It opens automatically on first boot after restart

steps.title: Create a Linux username and password
steps.detail: This account is separate from your Windows login

steps.title: You're in
steps.detail: You now have a real Linux terminal inside Windows

slides.narration: Here's the install, step by step. Open PowerShell as Administrator — right-click the Start button and choose Terminal, Admin. Then run one command: w-s-l space dash dash install. Restart when Windows asks you to. Ubuntu will finish setting itself up automatically and open a window asking you to create a Linux username and password — this is separate from your Windows login, so pick anything you'll remember. Once that's done, you're looking at a real Linux terminal running inside Windows.

slides.heading: Everyday WSL Commands
slides.subtitle: Run these from PowerShell or Windows Terminal

items.label: wsl -l -v
items.detail: List installed distros and which WSL version each uses

items.label: wsl
items.detail: Jump straight into your default Linux distro

items.label: wsl --shutdown
items.detail: Fully stop all running WSL instances

items.label: wsl --version
items.detail: Check your installed WSL and kernel version

slides.narration: A handful of commands cover almost everything you'll need day to day. w-s-l space dash-l space dash-v lists your installed distros. Just w-s-l on its own drops you straight into Ubuntu. w-s-l dash-dash shutdown fully stops everything if something gets stuck. dash-dash update keeps the engine itself current. And dash-dash version tells you exactly what you're running.

slides.heading: Checking Your Setup
slides.subtitle: wsl -l -v in action
slides.image_alt: Terminal output of wsl -l -v showing Ubuntu on WSL version 2
slides.narration: Running wsl dash-l dash-v confirms two things at a glance: that Ubuntu is installed, and that it's on version 2 — which is what you want. If it says version 1, something's off and it's worth re-running the installer.

slides.heading: Next Term
slides.definition: A free tool that downloads, runs, and manages AI language models on your own computer — no cloud account, no subscription, no API key.
items: Everything runs locally — your prompts never leave your machine
One command downloads a model, one command starts chatting
slides.narration: Next term: Ollama. It's a free tool that downloads, runs, and manages AI language models directly on your own computer — no cloud account, no subscription, no API key to sign up for. Everything happens locally, which means your prompts never leave your machine.

slides.heading: Install Ollama Inside WSL
slides.subtitle: One command

steps.title: Open your WSL Ubuntu terminal
steps.detail: Type wsl from PowerShell, or open “Ubuntu” from the Start menu

steps.title: Run the install script
steps.detail: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

steps.title: Wait for it to finish
steps.detail: It downloads Ollama and sets it up as a background service

steps.title: Confirm it installed
steps.detail: ollama --version

slides.narration: Installing Ollama inside WSL is one line. Open your Ubuntu terminal, then run: curl space dash f-s-s-capital L space the address https colon slash slash ollama dot com slash install dot s-h, piped to s-h. Let it finish — it sets Ollama up to run as a background service automatically. Confirm it worked with ollama space dash dash version.

slides.heading: The Install Script
slides.subtitle: curl ... | sh, running inside WSL
slides.image_alt: WSL terminal showing the Ollama install script downloading and configuring the service
slides.narration: Here's that install script running — it drops the ollama binary into place and starts the background service listening on port eleven-four-three-four, which is the address every Ollama command talks to under the hood.

slides.heading: Ollama Command Cheat Sheet
slides.subtitle: Everything starts with ollama
slides.code:
ollama serve                  # start the server (usually already running)
ollama pull llama3.2          # download a model without running it
ollama run llama3.2           # download (if needed) and start chatting
ollama list                   # show every model you've downloaded
ollama ps                     # show models currently loaded in memory
ollama show llama3.2          # see details about one model
ollama rm llama3.2            # delete a model you no longer need
ollama stop llama3.2          # unload a model from memory
items: pull downloads only; run downloads AND starts chatting
list shows what's on disk; ps shows what's loaded right now
rm deletes the model; stop just frees up memory
slides.narration: This is the whole cheat sheet. pull just downloads a model. run downloads it if needed and immediately starts a chat. list shows everything you've got on disk; p-s shows what's actually loaded in memory right now. show gives you details on one model. And rm deletes a model for good, while stop just frees the memory without deleting anything.

slides.heading: Which Model Should You Pick?
slides.subtitle: Match the model size to your hardware

columns.title: Best Quality — llama3.1:70b
points: Wants 64 GB+ RAM or a GPU
Slow on an ordinary laptop CPU

slides.narration: Model choice comes down to your hardware, not preference. llama3.2 at 3 billion parameters is small, fast, and fine on 8 gigabytes of RAM — great for testing. Mistral 7B or llama3.1 8B is the balanced middle ground, and honestly the sensible default if you've got 16 gigabytes. The 70 billion parameter version of llama3.1 is genuinely better, but it wants 64 gigabytes of RAM or a real GPU — don't try it on a laptop.

Once the progress bars finish, ollama space run space llama3 point 2 drops you straight into a chat — type a question, hit Enter, and the model answers right there in the terminal. When you're done, type slash bye to exit cleanly.

slides.narration: Last piece of vocabulary: OpenWebUI. It's a private, browser-based chat interface for whatever models Ollama is running — it looks and feels a lot like ChatGPT, except it's entirely yours, running entirely on your own machine.

slides.heading: Install Docker Desktop First
slides.subtitle: OpenWebUI runs inside a Docker container

steps.title: Download Docker Desktop
steps.detail: From docker.com, the Windows installer

steps.title: Run the installer
steps.detail: Keep “Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V” checked

steps.title: Restart Windows
steps.detail: When the installer prompts you

steps.title: Open Docker Desktop
steps.detail: Wait until it shows “Running” in the bottom-left

steps.title: Enable WSL integration
steps.detail: Settings → Resources → WSL Integration → toggle on Ubuntu

steps.title: Apply & Restart
steps.detail: Confirms the integration

slides.narration: OpenWebUI runs inside a Docker container, so Docker Desktop comes first. Download it from docker dot com, run the installer, and keep the “Use WSL 2” option checked. Restart when it asks. Once Docker Desktop is open and shows Running in the corner, go to Settings, Resources, WSL Integration, and turn the toggle on for Ubuntu. Click Apply and Restart to lock it in.

slides.heading: Turning On WSL Integration
slides.subtitle: Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → WSL Integration

cards.title: The toggle
points: Enable integration with your Ubuntu distro

cards.title: Why it matters
points: Lets Docker containers see your WSL environment

slides.image_alt: Docker Desktop settings screen with WSL integration enabled for Ubuntu
slides.narration: This toggle is the one setting that trips people up if it's missed — without it, Docker can't see your WSL environment at all. Flip it on for Ubuntu and you're set.

slides.heading: Run the OpenWebUI Container
slides.subtitle: One command, run from your WSL terminal
slides.code:
docker run -d \
  -p 3000:8080 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -v open-webui:/app/backend/data \
  --name open-webui \
  --restart always \
  ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
items: --add-host lets the container reach Ollama on WSL
-v open-webui:... saves your chats between restarts
--restart always brings it back after a reboot
slides.narration: This one docker run command does the whole job. The dash-p flag opens the interface at localhost port 3000. add-host lets the container reach out and find Ollama running on your WSL host. The dash-v flag saves your chat history so it survives restarts. And restart-always means it comes back on its own after a reboot, so you're not re-running this command every time.

slides.heading: Confirming It's Running
slides.subtitle: docker ps, right after launch

slides.image_alt: Terminal output of docker ps showing the open-webui container running
slides.narration: A quick docker space p-s confirms the container is actually up, with port 3000 mapped and ready — that's your green light to open a browser.

slides.heading: Quick Troubleshooting
slides.subtitle: The five snags almost everyone hits

items.label: “ollama: command not found”
items.detail: Close and reopen your WSL terminal so the install takes effect

items.label: OpenWebUI shows no models
items.detail: Run ollama list inside WSL to confirm a model is downloaded

items.label: Page won't load at localhost:3000
items.detail: Check Docker Desktop shows the container as “Running”

items.label: Everything feels slow
items.detail: Run wsl --shutdown, then reopen WSL for a clean restart

items.label: Model won't load / crashes
items.detail: It may be too large for your RAM — try a smaller model

slides.narration: A few snags cover almost every problem people hit. If ollama isn't found, just close and reopen your terminal. If OpenWebUI shows no models, check ollama list inside WSL first. If the page won't load, confirm Docker Desktop actually shows the container running. If things feel sluggish, wsl dash-dash shutdown and reopen gives you a clean restart. And if a model won't load at all, it's probably too big for your RAM — step down to a smaller one.

slides.closing_line: You're running a private AI, entirely on your own machine.
slides.closing_body: WSL gave you the Linux environment. Ollama gave you the models. OpenWebUI gave you the chat window. Revisit any command on this deck any time — nothing here ever needs the cloud.
slides.image_alt: Close-up of a glowing laptop keyboard
slides.narration: That's the whole path — WSL gave you a real Linux environment inside Windows, Ollama gave you the models and the commands to run them, and OpenWebUI gave you a proper chat window in your browser. Every command in this deck is yours to revisit any time, and none of it ever needs the cloud. Thanks for following along.
